How to use this template: replace every line in italics with your own writing, then delete the italics. Use it as it is, or as inspiration for your own layout. The headings follow the rubric, so each part maps to one grading row.

# Part 1: Codebook

## Study overview

*Name your research question or hypotheses, the material you are coding (platform, language, what was collected and how), and the time period (first and last date).*

## Unit of analysis

*State exactly what one coded item is (one post, one message, one minute of video), and say what is not part of it (replies, links, images). State it once. Every variable below is coded on this item.*

*List any fields you look up rather than code (an ID, a date, a count), and any measure you compute in R from your coded variables.*

## If your study uses more than one source

*Skip this section if all your material comes from one source.*

Write one codebook for each **unit of analysis**, not one for each platform. Two sources that share a unit share a codebook. Two sources with different units each get their own codebook, joined by a key.

| Your study | Units | Codebooks |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Spotify streaming numbers and TikTok videos that use the same songs | A song (Spotify) and a video (TikTok) | Two, linked by the song |
| Box office figures and published reviews of the same films | A film (box office) and a review (reviews) | Two, linked by the film |
| TikTok videos and Instagram Reels on the same topic, coded the same way | A short video, on both platforms | One, with a `platform` variable |

When you need two codebooks, repeat Part 1 for each one, then add a linking section:

### Linking the codebooks

| Element | Your entry |
|:--|:--|
| Key variable | *The variable that appears in both codebooks and names the same thing in each (for example, `song_id` or `film_title`). Define it in both codebooks, word for word.* |
| How records match | *Write the matching rule: spelling, capitalization, and how you treat remixes, re-releases, or two films with the same title. Write it as a rule: "If ..., match ...".* |
| How many to how many | *How many items in one codebook match one item in the other (one song to many TikTok videos; one film to many reviews).* |
| Records that do not match | *What you do with an item that has no partner in the other source: keep it, drop it, or code it separately. Say which and why.* |

The key is what lets you put the two sources side by side in R later: one table per codebook, joined on the key.

# Part 2: Reliability protocol

*Open with one sentence: you are the only coder, so every reliability claim here is about your own consistency over time, intracoder reliability (stability), not agreement between two coders.*

## 6. The statistic

*Name the statistic (for example, Krippendorff's alpha) and the metric for each variable, with one sentence on why this statistic and not another. Call it intracoder reliability (stability). Say why percent agreement alone is not enough.*

## 7. The threshold

*Give the threshold with its source (author, year). Add one sentence saying a stability figure is a weaker claim than agreement between two coders and will not be reported as if it were one.*

## 8. The stability procedure

*Say how many items you will re-code (at least 10 percent of your coded items), that you will re-code them yourself at least 48 hours after the first pass, and that your first codes will be hidden while you do.*

*Name the dated file in your repository that records this plan before the re-code (for example, `codebook/stability-plan.md`), committed before you start the second pass.*

## 9. A fresh reliability sample

*Describe a sample kept separate from the items you used to build and revise the codebook: its size, and how it is drawn (for example, a seeded random draw in R).*

```r
# a seeded draw of re-code items, kept apart from the items that built the codebook
set.seed(2026)
recode_items <- coded_items |>
  filter(!item_id %in% build_items$item_id) |>
  slice_sample(n = 15)
```

## 10. When it fails

*Say in advance what you do if a variable misses the threshold: which categories you revise, how, and what keeps the codebook from bending toward your own habits (for example, revising only from written rules and re-testing on a new sample).*

## 11. Reporting a disappointing number

*Commit to reporting the figure even if it is low, and write what you will say about it.*

## 12. Single-coder safeguards

*Name at least three safeguards you are actually using, each described as what you do. Choose from the rubric's list or add your own.*

3. *Safeguard, and what you do.*

*One paragraph, written as what you would do if this study had a second coder: how many items you would double-code, which statistic you would report, how you would train the coder and settle disagreements, and which finding is most at risk.*
